blocks.sourceSectionTitle: Five ways to be paid for hacking, ranked by how far they scale

rows: Your own pentest and audit boutique
Scalable
You set the price per engagement, add clients through referrals, and later hire testers or package repeat work such as a yearly retest.
Salaried pentester at a security firm, product company or large consultancy
Scalable with a business layer
Real client exposure and steady pay, but pay follows the firm's grade ladder. The layer is your own: a niche (web apps, Active Directory, mobile, cloud), a public reputation and later consulting.
Security training, content and workshops
Scalable with a business layer
Teaching what you can really do reaches many learners at once through batches, courses or corporate workshops.
Red team and vulnerability research
Not so scalable
A deep, small field. Very few roles, strong competition at the entry stage and a second, harder stage to reach senior research work.
Bug bounty hunting as your main income
Not so scalable
You are paid per accepted bug, not per hour, and duplicates and rejected reports earn nothing. Income depends on luck and on outpacing other hunters and now automated tools.
Your own pentest and audit boutique
Not a starter route. Clients need to trust you with their systems, so it comes after a track record, a sample report and a few referrals.
Salaried pentester at a security firm, product company or large consultancy
Rarely open to freshers with no proof. Most listings expect hands-on evidence, and many expect prior IT or security experience.
Security training, content and workshops
Needs real field work first. Teaching with no practice behind it is the exact thing that feeds the course scams below.
Red team and vulnerability research
Treat it as a later specialisation after years in pentesting, not as a first goal.
Bug bounty hunting as your main income
Works as proof and side income. Keep a salary or savings buffer. Do not quit a job for it.

blocks.heading: What Each Costs and Proves
blocks.sourceSectionTitle: CEH, eJPT, PNPT, OSCP: what each costs and proves

rows: CEH (EC-Council)
A 125-question multiple-choice knowledge exam of 4 hours. A separate 6-hour practical exam exists for the CEH Master level.

Official course listings start at USD 1,699 (on-demand) and USD 2,499 (live online). Eligibility is through official training or a request based on experience; EC-Council recommends at least 2 years of IT security experience.
eJPT (INE)
A hands-on, auto-graded entry exam at junior pentester level, covering host and network testing, assessment methods, auditing and web basics.
Sold inside INE bundles with an exam voucher. The INE page we read did not list a price, so check the checkout page.
PNPT (TCM Security)

A realistic test, not a flag-hunt: OSINT, Active Directory attack path, a written report and a live 15-minute debrief. Five days for the test plus two days for the report. AI tools are allowed if you disclose how you used them.
USD 499 for the exam voucher plus training, with one free retake (TCM Security page).
OSCP (OffSec)
A 24-hour proctored hands-on exam. No formal requirements, but OffSec strongly recommends TCP/IP basics, Windows and Linux administration, and Bash or Python.
USD 1,749 for course plus labs for 90 days plus one attempt; USD 2,749 a year for Learn One with two attempts; USD 1,699 for the exam alone (OffSec page).
CompTIA PenTest+
Up to 90 questions, mixed multiple choice and performance-based tasks, in 165 minutes. CompTIA recommends 3 to 4 years of pentesting experience plus Network+ and Security+.
The CompTIA page we read did not list the exam price.
CEH (EC-Council)
Good as a recognised line on a CV for listings that ask for it. On its own it does not prove you can break into a system, and the training fee is high.
eJPT (INE)
A sensible first practical badge. Shows you can do small, guided tasks.
PNPT (TCM Security)
Best proof per rupee at the junior stage, because the report and debrief are the real job.
OSCP (OffSec)
Widely named in pentest job listings, so check the ones you target. Worth it after you have lab hours, not before. A failed attempt on an unprepared first try is an expensive way to learn.
CompTIA PenTest+
Fits people who already work in security and want a vendor-neutral line. Not a fresher's first purchase.
BTech CS or IT student

Start the labs in the first year, not the last. Aim for a security or application-testing internship; ISC2's 2025 study found internships were rare (3% of respondents) yet had the highest recommendation rate (69%).
Spending most of the college budget on a security elective or a private bootcamp. Keep to roughly 10% of the family education budget for the degree.
BCA, BSc IT or any graduate
Build the networking and Linux base, then web testing. A degree name is not the filter; a write-up folder is.
Paying for a 'guaranteed placement' hacking course before you have finished the free labs.
Developer or software tester already working
You have the strongest start. Learn web attack basics on PortSwigger, test your own company's staging apps only with written approval, and move toward application security.
Testing live company systems with no sign-off because 'it is for the company's good'.
IT support or network staff
Your base is real. Add web and Active Directory practice and aim for a security operations role first, then pentesting.
Quitting a paid job for full-time practice with no lab proof yet.
Class 12 student, no technical base yet
Choose a degree that teaches computing and networks, and build the lab habit in parallel. A hacking certificate at 17 is not a plan.
Learning 'tricks' from videos without understanding the systems underneath them.

blocks.heading: Competition, Pay Signals and Bug Bounty Luck
blocks.sourceSectionTitle: Competition, pay signals and bug bounty luck

rows: Salaried penetration tester, India
We found no reliable public pay survey for Indian penetration testers, so we print no figure here.
Pay rises with proof and employer type. Check current job listings and ask for the range before you apply.
Bug bounty pool, worldwide
HackerOne bug bounty programs paid about USD 81 million over 12 months, reported in October 2025. The top 100 programs paid USD 51 million, about 63% of that.
Money is concentrated in a few large programs, and a long tail of hunters shares little. The average yearly payout per active program (about USD 42,000) is not what a hunter earns.
Top bug bounty earners
HackerOne says some researchers now pass six-figure annual earnings, while the top 100 all-time earners took USD 31.8 million in total.
That is the exceptional end of a very uneven field. It is not the median.
Skills over headcount
ISC2's 2025 study (16,029 respondents) found 59% report critical or significant skills needs, with AI (41%) and cloud security (36%) the top two. It no longer estimates a workforce gap.
Employers want specific, proven skills, not more badge holders.
'Become a hacker in a few weeks' or 'earn lakhs from bug bounty fast'
Skill and proof take longer for most people, and bounty income is uneven. A promise of speed is a sales line.
Teaching how to get into social media, WhatsApp or other people's accounts
That is unauthorised access, not ethical hacking. A course that teaches it is teaching offences.
A fee several times the OSCP bundle, with no lab you can try first
Compare with the listed fees above and the free labs. Ask to try a sample module before you pay.
Guaranteed placement or a 'government-recognised ethical hacker' title
No pass in a short course guarantees a job, and the recognised credentials are the vendor ones named above. Ask for named, checkable past learners.
No written scope, no mention of authorisation or the IT Act in the syllabus
A real course teaches the legal line on day one.
The only deliverable is a certificate
A certificate alone is weak proof. Look for graded labs, feedback on your reports and a project you can show.

blocks.heading: Who Should Skip Ethical Hacking
blocks.sourceSectionTitle: Who should skip ethical hacking, or choose another door

rows: You are drawn by the movie idea of hacking into anything
The job is scoped, written, authorised and report-heavy. Hacking without permission is the thing the career exists to oppose.
You dislike writing reports
The report is the product. A good test that is badly written is not paid well or rehired.
You want a quick fresher job with a fixed path
The offensive lane has few entry roles. A SOC or application security job is the more usual first door.
You cannot practise alone for long stretches
Most of the learning happens in your own lab, stuck on a problem, with no teacher in the room.
You plan to rely on bug bounty to pay your bills
Income per bug is uneven and a month can pay nothing. Keep a base income.
Class 12 student
Pick a computing degree and keep the education spend to about 10% of the family budget. Start free labs only after you can use Linux comfortably.
College student
Finish two web lab write-ups and publish them. Apply for a security internship with the links in your first message.
Fresher with no offer
Apply for application testing, SOC and security support roles, and keep your labs going. Plan the pentest move as the second job.
Working developer or tester
Learn web attack basics, get written approval to test staging systems, and ask your security team if you can shadow them.
Mid-career professional wanting a switch
Do not quit first. Build proof on evenings and weekends and talk to three working pentesters before spending on OSCP.
